subtype: Saying I love you and drawing [Expressing]
passage: Pradeep was away on a work trip, so Chaitanya, five, held her drawing up to the phone screen. It was an orange scribble with two stick people. "I love you, Papa. That's us." The connection blurred and she raised her voice. "I LOVE YOU!" Pradeep laughed. "I can see it, sweetheart." Next morning she said, "I don't love you, you're not here!" and then ran to fetch her orange pencil to draw him a bigger one.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya's drawing show?
qa.a: An orange scribble with two stick people.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when she said "I don't love you, you're not here!"?
qa.a: Missing him and upset about the distance, not ending her love. Fetching the pencil for a bigger drawing suggests the love is still strong.

qa.q: How could Pradeep respond to her words?
qa.a: Accept the feeling, tell her he misses her too, and keep the calls and drawings going.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when the connection blurs?
qa.a: Probably frustrated and a bit sad to be far away, yet warmed, since he laughs and says he can see it.

grounding: Shows a preschooler saying I love you and showing a drawing over a weak phone call, with words that swing with the moment.

subtype: Saying I love you and drawing [Expressing]
passage: Gautam, five, pressed a folded paper into his mother's hand as Jaya came home from the office. "For you. I love you. It's our house." Jaya opened it: four stick figures under a big sun, one taller than the house. "Which one is me?" "The tall one." She laughed and pinned it on the fridge. An hour later Gautam shouted, "I hate you!" about bath time, then tucked himself into her lap.

qa.q: Where did Jaya put the drawing?
qa.a: On the fridge.

qa.q: What might Gautam have meant by "I hate you" at bath time?
qa.a: A strong feeling in the moment about not wanting a bath, not a lasting one, as tucking himself into her lap suggests. He might also have been tired.

qa.q: How could Jaya respond to both "I love you" and "I hate you"?
qa.a: Take both as feelings of the moment, staying warm and calm and not holding him to either.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel pinning the drawing up?
qa.a: Touched and happy, perhaps tired after work. She laughed and put it where she would see it.

grounding: Shows a preschooler giving a drawing with I love you, with words that reflect strong feelings of the moment.

subtype: Saying I love you and drawing [Expressing]
passage:
“Papa, I love you a hundred thousand million!” Lalit threw his arms round Deepak's neck. “I'll never ever leave you, even when I'm big.”
“Never?”
“Never ever. I'll live in your room.”
Deepak laughed and hugged him. An hour later: “No ice cream before dinner.” Lalit stamped his foot. “I don't love you anymore!”
“Hmm. That's a big change,” said Deepak calmly.
At bedtime Lalit crept into his lap. “I love you again. A hundred thousand million.”
“I know,” said Deepak.

qa.q: Where did Lalit say he'd live when he's big?
qa.a: In Papa's room.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when he said “I don't love you anymore!”?
qa.a: He was angry and frustrated about the ice cream in that moment; it didn't mean his love had really gone.

qa.q: What did Deepak understand about Lalit's words, and how did he respond?
qa.a: He knew the words showed strong feelings of the moment, not fixed promises, so he stayed calm and warm.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel when Lalit says “I love you again” at bedtime?
qa.a: He probably feels touched and amused, knowing the love was always there.

grounding: A preschooler's I love you and I don't love you show strong feelings in the moment, and his father takes them calmly.

I love you more than Mummy.” I thanked him warmly and told him, “Your mummy is lucky to have your love too.” At pick-up, he ran to his mother shouting, “I love you most, Mummy!” Children his age say big words with big feeling. qa.a: He felt affection and warmth for Uma, and wanted to show it with a gift and big words.

qa.q: Why was Uma's reply wise?
qa.a: Uma thanked him warmly but gently reminded him that his mummy is lucky to have his love too, so his words didn't set up a rivalry.

qa.q: How might Yogesh's mother feel reading the note?
qa.a: She'd likely feel amused and reassured, knowing his big words are strong feelings of the moment.

grounding: The carer's note shows a preschooler saying I love you and giving a drawing, words that show strong feelings in the moment.

subtype: Saying I love you and drawing [Expressing]
passage: On the way to the village school, Hafsa picked a fistful of yellow wildflowers from the ditch. She gave them to Ankita Ma'am at the gate, stems dripping. “For you. I love you, Ma'am. When I'm big I'll marry you.” The other children giggled. Ankita crouched and took the flowers carefully. “Thank you, Hafsa. These are beautiful. I love teaching you.” She put them in a steel tumbler on her desk. Hafsa checked on them three times that morning.

qa.q: Where did Ankita Ma'am put the flowers?
qa.a: In a steel tumbler on her desk.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when she gave the flowers?
qa.a: She felt deep affection for her teacher and wanted to show it with a gift and big words.

qa.q: How did Ankita Ma'am respond to Hafsa's big promise?
qa.a: She accepted the flowers warmly and said she loved teaching her, gently taking the feeling without the promise.

qa.q: How might the other children see Hafsa's big promise?
qa.a: They found it funny, which is why they giggled, while Ankita Ma'am took the feeling behind it seriously.

grounding: A child shows love with wildflowers and a big promise, and her teacher receives the feeling kindly.

subtype: Saying I love you and drawing [Expressing]
passage:
In the kitchen in Seville, Hana handed Pablo a crumpled drawing: a tall stick man with a huge red heart for a body.

"That's you, Abuelo. I love you forever and ever, a hundred million."

Pablo pinned it to the fridge with the lemon magnet. "And I love you."

An hour later, when he said it was bath time, Hana stamped her foot. "I don't love you anymore!"

Pablo just ran the water.

Wrapped in a towel afterwards, she climbed onto his lap. "I love you again. And I love the ice-cream man too."

Pablo laughed. "Of course you do."

qa.q: What did Pablo use to pin the drawing to the fridge?
qa.a: The lemon magnet.

qa.q: What was Hana feeling when she said, "I don't love you anymore!"?
qa.a: She was most likely annoyed and frustrated about bath time, and her words showed that feeling in the moment, not a real change in love. Climbing onto his lap later shows she still felt close to him.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Pablo didn't take the angry words to heart and just ran the bath, because he understood they were a flash of feeling, not a promise.

qa.q: How does Pablo see Hana's "I love you forever" and "I don't love you anymore"?
qa.a: He sees both as big feelings of the moment, so he enjoys the love and laughs off the anger.

grounding: It shows a preschooler saying "I love you" and drawing a picture for her grandfather, with words that carry strong feelings in the moment rather than fixed promises.
